learningObjective: Identify the benefits and costs of function inlining and the conditions when it may be inhibited.

canonicalClaims.claim: Inlining removes call/return overhead and enables cross-call optimizations (constant propagation, CSE, LICM), but has costs: increased code size, potential icache pressure, higher register pressure, and longer compile times; indirect calls require devirtualization before inlining.
conditions: The caller's compilation unit can see the callee body (or LTO makes it visible).
The inlining heuristic decides the benefit outweighs the cost.
nonImplications: Does not imply larger inlining budgets always improve performance.
Does not imply recursion prevents all inlining; bounded partial inlining is possible.

misconceptions.claim: Recursive functions can never be inlined.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Bounded partial inlining is possible (e.g., a few levels deep); unbounded recursion cannot be fully inlined but can still benefit from targeted specialization.
Aggressive inlining can inflate icache footprint and register pressure, slowing execution.

misconceptions.claim: Indirect calls can be inlined without devirtualization.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Inlining requires a statically known target; indirect calls need devirtualization or profiling-guided speculative inlining first.

implementationFacts: LLVM inliner: cost-benefit heuristic based on caller/callee size, argument constants, and cold/hot annotations.
PGO (profile-guided optimization) informs the inliner about hot call sites.
attribute((always_inline)) and noinline override the heuristic.
performanceScenarios: Small, hot accessors and inlined lambda callbacks benefit from inlining; large virtual dispatch tables often benefit from profile-guided devirtualization + inlining.
